title: Grace-persuasion fiducia: primary essential act, or only perfection’s fruit?
source_text: XCIX. Sed praecipua quaestio est de fiducia sumpta secundo modo, videlicet pro firma illa persuasione qua quis statuit gratiam se a Deo consecutum esse, & bona Evangelio promissa ad se pertinere. Multi ut supra ostendimus, ab hac fiducia fidem definiunt, & sic loquuntur quasi fides salvifica & justificans sine illa constare non posset, & vocant illam partem fidei primariam, & praecipuum atque specificum fidei salvificae actum, ut videre est in iis quae ante relata sunt ex Roberto Baronio, Riveto, Ursino, Paraeo, Wendelino, & aliquot aliis. Alii vero contra contendunt talem fiduciam & persuasionem, ad fidei quidem perfectionem, sed non ad intimam ejus essentiam spectare; illam esse quid proprium fidei corroboratae, sed non fidei infirmae; multos ad vere fidelium justificatorum numerum pertinere, qui tamen fiducia illa destituti sunt: proinde vocant illam fidei salvificae actum accidentalem, & non essentialem; non primarium, sed secundarium; non directum, sed reflexum: & censent illam rectius dici fructum & effectum fidei, quam praecipuum ejus actum. Ut manifestum est ex iis quae prolixe satis citavimus ex Perkinsio, Amesio, Davenantio, Wittichio, Widmario, Petro Molinaeo filio, & Anglicana ipsa Confessione Anni 1647.
pass_a_gloss: But the chief question is concerning trust taken in the second mode, namely for that firm persuasion by which one lays down that he has obtained grace from God, and that the goods promised in the Gospel pertain to himself. Many, as we showed above, define faith from this trust, and so speak as if saving and justifying faith could not stand without it, and call it the primary part of faith, and the chief and specific act of saving faith, as is to be seen in those things formerly related from Robert Baron, Rivetus, Ursinus, Paraeus, Wendelin, and some others. But others on the contrary contend that such trust and persuasion pertains indeed to the perfection of faith, but not to its inmost essence; that it is something proper to corroborated faith, but not to weak faith; that many belong to the number of the truly faithful justified who nevertheless are destitute of that trust: accordingly they call it an accidental, not essential, act of saving faith; not primary, but secondary; not direct, but reflex: and they judge that it is more rightly called a fruit and effect of faith than its chief act. As is plain from those things which we have cited at sufficient length from Perkins, Ames, Davenant, Wittich, Widmar, Peter du Moulin the son, and the English Confession itself of the Year 1647.
pass_b_english: Chief quarrel: second-sense fiducia = firm persuasion that I have obtained grace and that Gospel goods are mine.
Baron, Rivetus, Ursinus, Paraeus, Wendelin (and others): define faith by it; call it primary, chief, specific saving act — as if saving faith could not stand without it.

Perkins, Ames, Davenant, Wittich, Widmar, young du Moulin, English Confession 1647: it belongs to faith’s perfection, not inmost essence; proper to corroborated, not weak, faith; many truly justified lack it.
So: accidental/secondary/reflex act — better called faith’s fruit than its chief act.
